Yep. so I will first talk a little bit about the context, the background. so over years, people have been-- So this, this, this paper is more vision-focused. over years, people have been developing larger and larger datasets and, from more and more diverse sources. For example, initially we had MNIST, and then CIFAR, and then ImageNet, and then this internet scale datasets like, DataCamp or, Conceptual Captions, CC, dataset from Google. And they have more and more, seemingly more and more diverse images, and they are larger and larger to the billion, from, from like, tens of thousands to billion scale. And, it's, it's, it was kind of tempting to make the assumption that we are good, already good with datasets because it's really all the things you can get from internet, from these datasets. but in some of our initial experiments, we found that these datasets are nothing, still nothing like each other.

And how, how do we measure this? We, we designed a very dumb experiment that's, doesn't make sense at all as a, as a, like, a deep learning training, program. What we did is this. given three very large scale computer vision datasets, we train and classify neural network to classify, to classify which, which dataset a given particular image comes from. It's not a practical problem, it's just to try to guess the dataset's origin. it's a multi-ca- multiclass classification problem. It turns out, even with these seemingly non-- very diverse datasets, the model can still tell this answer with surprisingly high accuracy, up to, more, higher than 80% accuracy when, when you have three datasets.

So the random guessing accuracy will be 33%, but in fact, the model can be, much better, than that. So this say, this means to a model, these datasets still, are still very, very different. It has very clear cues for the model to tell which dataset this, this image comes from. Of course, we are doing this on held out validation sets. We are not, like, predicting the training, training images. but still, this has been surprisingly high, surprisingly accurate, and, that like prompts us to reflect, are we really su- have we, we really been successful in curating a large scale, all-encompassing dataset, at least in computer vision domain? What, and what, what kind of dataset is the end goal?

It's kind of hard to define this so-called all-encompassing global distribution dataset. Different people might have different criterion, and it might not be a reasonable assumption there. So should we-- So because, a big story of the success of LM is that it can do-- It's not a, like, domain-specific, specific model, right? So we want the model to be able to do everything, and in order for that to happen, we need a model,... a common assumption is that we need the model to, to have seen everything during training. And how, how, how, how much progress are we making on that? It seems from this initial experiment that we, we haven't, reached that point, yet, and still makes sense to think about how do we curate these datasets for, for the model to be really generalizing, to, to every task we want the model to be good at.

Yeah.

astra.text:
Mm-hmm. Yeah. So the motivation is, we talk about data becoming larger and larger, but does larger necessarily mean more diverse, or more representative of the world? I think that's a question we should ask, especially if we believe data is such an important component of these models.

So dataset bias, here, means that every dataset has its own distribution. When you collect images, you make choices, right? Where do you collect them from? What do you search for? How do you filter them? And these choices affect what kinds of images end up in your dataset. So a model can perform very well on a test set collected in the same way, but when you move to another dataset, the performance may change. And then the question is, how much has the model learned that generalizes beyond that particular collection of data?

This is an old concern in computer vision. And what we wanted to revisit is, now that we have much larger datasets, and we're collecting data from more sources, have we actually addressed this problem? It's tempting to think that once you have enough images from the internet, these differences will kind of disappear. But that's something we need to investigate.

One way to make the question concrete is to ask whether you can recognize which dataset an image comes from. So instead of asking what object is in the image, you ask where the image was collected. If a model can distinguish the datasets, that tells us there are systematic differences in their distributions. Then we still need to understand what those differences are and how they affect learning.

So, yeah, the motivation connects to what we were discussing earlier. Once we say data matters, we need to look beyond the number of examples. We need to understand what we're collecting, what we're leaving out, and whether the resulting model works on the data we actually care about.

sol.text:
Mm-hmm. Yeah. So the motivation is exactly connected to what we were just discussing. If data is the important component, then we need to understand whether two datasets that are supposedly describing the same visual world are actually interchangeable. And dataset bias is this old observation that they are not: the way images are collected, filtered, labeled, and even what people choose to photograph leaves a very recognizable signature.

So we wanted to revisit this question because today the datasets are much larger and more diverse, and one might expect that internet-scale collection has made the old problem disappear. What we found is that it really has not. Even across generations of datasets, models can still identify which dataset an image came from, and a model trained on one distribution does not necessarily transfer equally well to another. So scale alone does not automatically give you an unbiased or universal representation.

And to me, the important lesson is that a dataset is not just a large bag of examples. All of those collection and curation decisions define what the model learns—sometimes as much as an architectural choice would. That was why we called it a decades-long battle: the models and datasets have changed enormously, but this very basic issue remains. Before asking only how many more tokens or images we need, we should ask which data we are scaling, what is missing from it, and what biases the collection pipeline is repeatedly introducing. Yeah.

opus.text:
Mm-hmm. Yeah, so that work, the, the motivation actually goes back to a paper I really love, which is Torralba and Efros' "Unbiased Look at Dataset Bias" from 2011. And in that paper, they had this, kind of playful, but very insightful game called "Name That Dataset." So you take images from, at that time, like a dozen different computer vision datasets — Caltech, PASCAL, ImageNet, and so on — and you strip away the labels, and you just train a classifier to predict which dataset each image came from. And back then with, like, classical features, HOG, GIST, they could do this way, way above chance. And the conclusion was, each dataset has its own signature, its own bias, its own, kind of, fingerprint.

So the reason we wanted to revisit this, is that a decade later, everything about how we build datasets has changed, right? Back then, datasets were curated, they were, they were, you know, hand-collected, tens of thousands of images, a lot of human decisions involved in what goes in. And today, we, we scrape the internet. We have hundreds of millions, billions of images, very diverse, supposedly, supposedly much less curated. So the, the natural hope, and I think a lot of people implicitly assume this, is that, okay, at this scale, bias should be, kind of, washed out. Like, if you're taking everything from the internet, what, what bias could there be?

So we just, we just played the same game. We took three large-scale datasets — YFCC, CC, which is Conceptual Captions, and DataComp — and we trained a model to do three-way classification, which dataset does this image come from. Chance is 33%. And the model gets above 84% on held-out validation images. Which was, honestly, much higher than what we expected when we started. Mm. And for comparison, we also asked humans to play, and humans are, are around 40-something percent. So the, the network is seeing something we, we largely cannot.

And then of course the immediate objection is, okay, maybe it's a shortcut, maybe it's JPEG artifacts, maybe it's resolution, maybe it's, some low-level signature from the collection pipeline. So we did quite a lot of control experiments. we, we did heavy augmentation, we, we downsampled to very low resolution, we used only patches, we tried different architectures, and, the accuracy stays high. And, and importantly, we did a, kind of pseudo-dataset control where you take one single dataset and randomly split it into three parts and call them three datasets — and there, the model can't do better than chance. So it's, it's, it's not an artifact of the setup.

And then the, the part that I find most interesting is, the features the model learns from playing this game, they're semantic. They transfer to downstream tasks reasonably. So the bias is not just, like, a watermark in the corner. It's, it's in the content, in, in what kind of pictures end up in each dataset. So the, the answer to "are we there yet" is, is pretty clearly no. Yeah.

grok.text:
Yeah. Yeah, so this one is a, is a really interesting story as well. So the original paper is from, I think, 2011, Torralba and Efros, Unbiased Look at Dataset Bias. And they had this very clever, very simple experiment, which is, can you name the dataset from a single image? Like, you show a photo, and you ask a classifier, did this come from ImageNet, from PASCAL, from Caltech, from LabelMe, and so on. And the answer was yes, very easily. You can tell which dataset it came from. And that was kind of a wake-up call that our datasets have very strong, distinctive biases. Photographer bias, selection bias, how objects are centered, the backgrounds, the low-level statistics, all of that.

So a decade later, we have much larger datasets, much better models, internet-scale data, and people might think, okay, maybe this problem is gone. Maybe now that everything is so big and so diverse, the bias is washed out. So we wanted to revisit this question: are we there yet? Has this decade of progress actually solved dataset bias?

And what we found is, unfortunately, no. We can still train a classifier to tell which dataset an image came from, and with modern neural networks, it’s actually even easier. The accuracy is extremely high, even on these large-scale modern datasets that people use today. The signature of the dataset is still very much there. Even if you try to control for the object categories, even if the datasets are supposed to cover similar things, the model can still pick it up.

So the motivation was really just, this is such a classic question, and we wanted to know whether the field has actually made progress on this particular problem, or whether we’ve been, kind of, the models got better, the datasets got bigger, but the underlying bias is still sitting there. And I think the lesson is closer to the second. Yeah.

gemini.text:
Yeah. So that paper was really inspired by a very classic paper from 2011 by Antonio Torralba and Alexei Efros, called "An Unbiased Look at Dataset Bias." 

Back then, in the pre-deep learning era, they showed that vision datasets had strong inherent biases. They designed this famous "Name That Dataset" experiment, where a classifier could easily tell which dataset an image came from just based on subtle collection biases and quirks, and they also showed that when you train a model on one dataset and test it on another, the performance drops significantly.

And then, over the past decade, deep learning completely revolutionized computer vision. We got ConvNets, vision transformers, large-scale ImageNet pre-training, and much better optimization. And there was this general belief or assumption in the community that deep representations, because they learn rich visual features from data, had largely solved or at least mitigated dataset bias. People assumed modern models learn more invariant, general representations.

So our motivation was to ask: after a decade of deep learning, where are we really? Have we actually won that battle against dataset bias? So we essentially revisited those classic experiments using modern deep networks, modern training recipes, and modern representations. And what we found was that, surprisingly, dataset bias is still very much alive. Even modern deep models can still easily "name that dataset" with very high accuracy, and the cross-dataset generalization drop is still substantial. 

So it shows that simply changing or scaling architectures doesn't automatically solve the bias in our data, which goes back to the point that data itself, and understanding what is inside the data, is really the critical component we need to pay attention to.

kimi.text:
Mm-hmm. Yeah. So, so this is a very fun work for me, actually. So, so the, the background is a classic paper from, from 2011, by, Antonio Torralba and Alyosha Efros, called "Unbiased Look at Dataset Bias." And back then they did this, very fun, but also kind of thought provoking experiment. they, they played this game called "name the dataset." so you, you take images from the, the popular datasets back then, like, Caltech, LabelMe, PASCAL, and, and you ask a human, or you train a small classifier to guess, which dataset does this image come from? And, and it turns out it works way above chance. And, and more importantly, they showed that, if you train a model to recognize, say, cars on one dataset, and you test it on, another dataset that also has cars, the performance drops, dramatically. So the, the picture they painted was, was pretty dark. every dataset carries its own bias from how it was collected, the camera, the web sources, the annotation process, whatever, and our models are, are just picking up these, these shortcuts. so we are not really learning about the visual world, we are just learning about, about the, the dataset.

so, so the motivation for our paper is, well, it's been more than ten years, right? Everything has changed. the datasets went from, like, tens of thousands of images to, to billions of images, and, the training changed from supervised training on one dataset to, to self-supervised or language-supervised pretraining on internet scale data. So the, the natural question is, to, to quote our title, are we there yet? Is dataset bias still a problem?

so, we kind of systematically re-ran these experiments with, with modern models and modern datasets. And I think the, the answer is, is nuanced, is two-sided. on one hand, the bias is still there. you can take the frozen features of a very strong model, and you can still name the dataset with, with pretty high accuracy. so, so the signature of the dataset is, is still sitting there in the representation. But, but on the other hand, the consequence of the bias is much, much less severe now. the cross-dataset generalization gap has, has narrowed a lot, especially for models trained on, very large and very diverse data.

And, and for me, connecting back to what we discussed before, the biggest lever here is, is again, the data. like, the very naive idea they proposed back in 2011, just, just train on the union of many datasets, turns out to work, really well if you do it at, at internet scale. It's the, the diversity of the data, not the architecture, not some clever debiasing algorithm, that, that is winning this battle. so I, I wouldn't say the battle is fully won, but we are, we are much closer, and, and the weapon turned out to be just, more diverse data. and I think also it's a, a lesson for evaluation, like we, we should always evaluate across multiple datasets, not, not only inside one benchmark. Yeah.

fable.text:
Mm-hmm. Yes. So, so this was a work with, with Kaiming, Kaiming He, when we were both at, at Meta. So the, the story goes back to, uh, 2011. There was this very famous paper by, by Antonio Torralba and, and Alexei Efros called "Unbiased Look at Dataset Bias." And, and in that paper, they, they proposed this, this kind of game, they call it the "Name That Dataset" game. So you take images from, from different datasets at that time, like Caltech 101, PASCAL VOC, um, SUN, LabelMe, these, these kind of datasets, and you ask, can you tell which dataset this image comes from? And, and the finding was, yes, it's, it's surprisingly easy. Like, even, even humans can do that reasonably well, and, and a simple classifier at that time can, can do very well. So each dataset has its own, kind of, signature, its own bias. And, and the, the conclusion was, this is, this is a problem, right? Because the models trained on one dataset do not generalize to, to the other.

So, so that was over a decade ago. And since then, the, the community has put in a lot of effort into, into building better datasets. So the, the datasets now are, are much larger, much more diverse, they're, they're scraped from the internet, they're, they're less curated, right? Like, YFCC, like, LAION, DataComp, these, these are hundreds of millions or billions of images. So, so the natural assumption would be, okay, this bias problem should be, should be largely gone now, because, because these datasets are all just, kind of, random samples of the internet. So, so we wanted to just, just revisit that, revisit the same question. Are we there yet? Like, after, after a decade of, of battles, is, is dataset bias still, still a thing?

So, so the setup is very simple. We, we took, um, three, three large-scale datasets, um, YFCC, CC, which is Conceptual Captions, and, and DataComp, so we call that combination YCD. And we just train a network to, to classify which dataset each image comes from. Three-way classification. So, so if there's no bias, you'd expect, like, chance level, thirty-three percent, right? And, and it turns out the model can do that with, with very high accuracy, like above eighty percent, on, on held-out data. And, and this is, this is with, with modern networks, with, with, um, ConvNeXt, with ViT, it doesn't really matter. It, it also works when you, when you do very aggressive data augmentation, when you, when you do self-supervised pre-training. It, it still works. And, and we also, um, we asked humans to, to play the same game, and, and humans are, are much worse. Like, humans are, are close to, to chance, slightly above. So, so the model is picking up on, on something that, that is really hard for, for us to, to see.

And, and one, one thing I, I found very interesting is, the features learned from this, from this dataset classification task, they're, they're actually semantically meaningful. So if you take that, that model and, and do linear probing on, on ImageNet, it, it actually transfers reasonably well. So, so the bias is, is not just, like, some low-level, like, JPEG artifact or, or, or resolution thing. It's, it's about the, the content, like what, what kind of objects, what kind of scenes, what, what kind of, um, styles each, each dataset tends to have. So, so I think the, the lesson is, yeah, dataset bias is, is still very much there, even, even with these, these very large, very diverse datasets. Um, but, but whether that's, that's a bad thing, that's, that's a, a separate question, right? Like, like, um, each dataset just has its own, kind of, distribution, and, and maybe that's, that's just the nature of, of data. But, but at least we, we should be aware of it, when we, when we say, oh, we train on, on internet-scale data, so, so it's, it's unbiased. It, it's not. Yeah.
